children: On the heels of its biggest acquisition to date, IonQ used its investor day to showcase its expanding presence in the quantum sector, including new product rollouts and a boost to its financial outlook.

IonQ's recent acquisition of SkyWater Technology prompted a bump to its guidance. The company raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $450 million and $460 million, up from a prior range of $280 million to $290 million before the transaction.

Analysts had anticipated updated figures ahead of the event. StoneX analyst Gary Mobley said last week that he expected the focus to center heavily on the transaction-IonQ's largest to date at $1.8 billion. Mobley predicts the deal could accelerate IonQ's road map for a 200,000-qubit system by roughly a year.

The deal aligns with the quantum technology company's ambition to become the industry's largest "merchant supplier," as CEO Niccolo de Masi puts it. IonQ stands as the largest pure-play quantum company by market capitalization, backed by a loyal retail investor base and a growing roster of commercial clients.

The SkyWater acquisition dominated the conversation on Tuesday as IonQ unveiled Superion, its sixth-generation quantum system. Featuring processors fabricated directly by SkyWater, the system is currently available for order with shipments slated for 2027.

Rosenblatt analyst John McPeake, who attended the event, believes the company is "deep into the productization part of the development cycle" based on comments by Chris Ballance, the company's president of quantum computing.

Ballance previously served as CEO of Oxford Ionics, a U.K.-based startup acquired by IonQ last year. The deal gave IonQ access to proprietary technology that later helped it claim a record in quantum performance.

While that acquisition strengthened its hardware capabilities and accelerated its work on larger systems, IonQ has since shifted its focus beyond computing to adjacent technologies like networking and cybersecurity.

As part of the investor event, the company announced an $8.18 million security agreement with enterprise data management firm Congruity360, which IonQ called "one of the largest commercial quantum-security agreements in the United States to date."
The company's expansion has coincided with growing federal interest in the technology, as Washington looks to it as both a commercial pursuit as well as a national security priority.

As recently as Tuesday, the government reinforced its focus on bolstering supply chains as the Commerce Department finalized agreements with several public companies. Rigetti Computing, D-Wave Quantum, and Quantinuum will trade equity for $100 million each in funding through the 2022 Chips and Science Act.

IonQ was notably absent from the Commerce Department deal when it was announced in May, a decision de Masi attributes to regulations restricting equity issuance while the SkyWater merger awaited approval.

"I don't think the government thinks IonQ needs $100 million when we raised $3.4 billion last year," de Masi added. Well-capitalized after several strategic equity raises, the company has its sights set elsewhere.

De Masi says that IonQ remains a key government partner, with a dedicated federal division and ongoing agency contracts. The CEO urges investors to watch the company's next moves closely. "As we are in more vectors of growth, there are more ways for us to partner with this nation's government and with enterprise customers," he said.
